readerTitle: The cleaning job that takes three hours never happens
caseNote: 실제 연구 (1950년대 미 공군 조종사 신체 측정, Gilbert Daniels) + 가상 사례 (청소 서비스, 물류 창고) · 가상 사례 수치는 설명용
insight: 평균을 보면 먼저 '이 숫자 뒤에 어떤 모양의 분포가 숨어 있나'를 묻는다. 평균에 딱 맞는 고객이나 작업은 하나도 없을 수 있다.
misconception: 평균값에 맞춰 계획하면 대부분의 경우에 맞는다.

sources.text: Daniels, G. S. (1952). The "Average Man"? Technical Note WCRD 53-7, Wright Air Development Center, U.S. Air Force.
Rose, T. (2016). The End of Average. HarperOne. (Daniels 연구의 대중적 소개)
청소 서비스와 물류 창고 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Daniels 연구: 조종사 4,063명, 신체 치수 10개, 각 치수의 중간 30% 범위를 '평균'으로 정의, 10개 모두 평균 범위에 든 사람은 0명. 1차 자료(1952 기술 보고서)로 수치를 다시 확인하세요.
이후 공군이 조절식 좌석 등 '조절 가능한 설계' 쪽으로 갔다는 내용은 주로 Todd Rose(2016)의 설명에 근거합니다. 카드에는 일반적으로만 적었습니다. 인과와 시기를 단정하지 않도록 확인하세요.
청소 계산: 소형 아파트 2시간 × 절반, 대형 주택 4시간 × 절반 → 평균 (2+4)÷2 = 3시간. 대형 주택이 3시간 슬롯에 들어가면 1시간 지연, 다음 작업으로 이어짐.

cards.title: The cleaning job that takes three hours never happens
body: A home cleaning company knows its average job takes three hours. So it books every visit in a three-hour slot.
Crews are late almost every afternoon. Customers complain. The average is correct. The schedule still fails.

image.label: A cleaning van stuck behind a clock showing three hours
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 청소 업체 밴과 직원 두 명이 문 앞에서 시계를 보며 초조해하는 장면. 벽에 붙은 일정표에는 똑같은 3시간 칸이 줄지어 있고 뒤쪽 칸들이 밀려 겹쳐 있음. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: Why are the crews running late?
body: The three-hour average comes from a full year of real jobs. Crews aren't wasting time, and no single job looks unusual.

options.text: The crews are getting slower and need more training
options.feedback: Training costs money and time, and it won't help if the crews are already working at a normal pace. The problem may be the plan, not the people.

options.text: Few jobs actually take three hours; most are much shorter or much longer
options.feedback: Right. A three-hour average can come from jobs that never take three hours. Long jobs overrun their slots, and the delay rolls into the rest of the day.

options.text: Three hours is too tight; add 15 minutes to every slot
options.feedback: A buffer softens the lateness, but it wastes time on short jobs and still isn't enough for long ones. It treats the average as the truth, just a bit padded.

cards.title: Two kinds of job, zero three-hour jobs.
body: Half the jobs are small apartments. Half are large houses. The average lands where no real job sits. Each large house runs **an hour over** its slot, and the next customer waits.

breakdown.label: The average
breakdown.detail: A job length that almost never happens

breakdown.label: Each large house
breakdown.detail: Late by an hour, pushing back the next visit

cards.title: Averages hide the story
body: An average squeezes many numbers into one. It tells you the middle. It does not tell you **how spread out** the numbers are, whether there are separate groups, or whether a few extremes are pulling it.
Before you plan around an average, look at the numbers behind it. A quick list or a simple chart is often enough. Ask three questions: How wide is the spread? Are there clusters? Are there outliers?

image.label: Two hills of job lengths with the average between them
image.brief: 히스토그램 인포그래픽. 가로축은 작업 시간(1~5시간). 2시간과 4시간 부근에 높은 봉우리 두 개, 3시간 지점에는 거의 막대가 없음. 3시간 위치에 점선과 "Average" 라벨.

cards.title: The Air Force's average pilot didn't exist.
body: Around 1950, U.S. Air Force researcher Gilbert Daniels measured 4,063 pilots on 10 body dimensions used in cockpit design, such as height and arm length.
He asked how many pilots fell near the average on all ten. The answer was **none**. A cockpit built for the average pilot fit no actual pilot.
The Air Force later moved toward designs that adjust to the person, such as adjustable seats.

image.label: Pilots of many shapes beside one rigid cockpit seat
image.brief: 1950년대 느낌의 일러스트. 키와 체형이 다른 조종사 다섯 명이 고정된 조종석 하나 앞에 서 있고, 누구에게도 맞지 않는 모습. 실제 군 휘장이나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A few big numbers can drag the middle.
body: An accounting firm says its average client pays $20,000 a year. But two large clients pay most of that. A typical client pays far less, and losing one big client would hurt more than the average suggests.
When a few values are extreme, the **median**, the value in the middle of the list, often describes the typical case better.
cards.softwareNote: "Average revenue per user" often hides a small group of heavy spenders and a large group paying little. Pricing or features built for the average user may suit neither group.

cards.title: Averages still have a job.
body: When the numbers sit close together, the average is a fine summary. And when you only care about totals, such as how much detergent to buy for a thousand jobs, the average does the work.
Averages fail when you plan for *each* case: one slot, one promise, one product size. That's when the spread matters. Look at it once before you commit.

cards.title: Now it's a warehouse.
body: Your warehouse ships orders nationwide. Average delivery time is about three days. But 70% of orders arrive in two days, and 30% go to remote areas and take five.
Marketing wants a delivery promise on the website. What do you choose?

options.text: Promise 3-day delivery everywhere, since that's the average
options.feedback: It matches the data on paper, but every remote order, nearly a third of the total, arrives late. You'd break a promise on thousands of orders.

options.text: Show the promise by region: 2 days for most, 5 days for remote areas
options.feedback: Each customer sees a promise that fits their case. It takes a little more setup, but most customers get a faster promise and nobody gets a false one.

options.text: Promise 5 days everywhere to be safe
options.feedback: You'll rarely be late, but you undersell your speed to 70% of customers who could hear "2 days". Safe, at the cost of looking slower than you are.

cards.title: Before trusting an average, look at what's behind it.
body: An average can describe nobody. Check the spread, the clusters and the outliers before you plan one slot, one price or one promise around it.
**Try it today:** pick one average you use often, such as job length, order size or delivery time. List twenty real values behind it. Does any group sit far from the average?
